blocks.p: By now, you've probably learned about the Polyvagal Theory: how your nervous system shifts between safety, flight, fight, and shutdown. And now you're asking yourself, okay, now what?

You're not alone. Understanding why and how your body reacts the way it does is really useful, and it can be validating and normalizing as a new piece of knowledge. But the real transformation happens when you apply that knowledge to your daily life. This is the first of five small, actionable tips for applying the Polyvagal Theory every day.

By the end of this one, you'll better understand the polyvagal primary and mixed states, and you'll be able to identify which state you spend the most time in. Knowing your state helps, because you might know what to do next based on that state's needs. And if you have that, you have a potential avenue for self-regulation.

blocks.h: Why identifying your state is hard

blocks.p: You've learned about the polyvagal autonomic states. Great. But identifying them, and how they show up in your real life, might be difficult. Especially if you have a hard time identifying how you feel or recognizing your emotions. On top of that, can you identify which state you spend the most time in? Can you spot when your safety state is active, and how much of it is active? It's also common to get confused by these states and how they present, like the difference between freeze and shutdown in particular.

So I'm going to lead you through all of the official polyvagal primary and mixed states. I'll also add one more, which will make complete sense, though it's not an official polyvagal mixed state. Perhaps someday it will be.
Here's how it works: I'll ask you a question, then follow it with a brief explanation to help you answer it.

You might be ready to connect with your environment, with yourself, or with others. You connect with the environment by mindfully using your senses. You connect with yourself by mindfully experiencing your inner sensations. And you connect with others through co-regulation.

Connecting with the environment could be smelling a candle, tasting a peach, looking out your window at the horizon, or watching rain fall into your pool. No matter what it is, you connect with the environment by using your senses mindfully.

Connecting with yourself could look like noticing what you feel when you connect with your environment. When you smell the candle, what does that trigger within? How does your body respond when you taste the peach, or look out at the horizon or the rainfall? Do you feel lighter? Is breathing easier? Are you more likely to smile? Do you want to mobilize, or stay put and expand your mindfulness? Connecting with yourself is connecting with the inner sensations of what it is to be you in the present moment. You can also connect with yourself by looking inward at your emotions and mindfully experiencing them, and this includes even the difficult ones.
Connecting with others can look like hugging, smiling, making eye contact, or reaching out to somebody you haven't spoken to in a while.

If you said yes to connecting with the environment, yourself, or others, you likely have lots of safety state activation. Congrats. That means your body has enough activity in its ventral vagal pathways to open up these avenues for connection. In the safety state, you're not only ready to connect or receive connection. You might also be ready to play with somebody else, relax with a book, or even work on a project.

blocks.h3: 2. Do you feel like escaping or aggressing?

blocks.p: Maybe you don't have that connection impulse. Maybe you feel more like escaping, or being aggressive. You might need space. Leaving a situation directly gives you space. Being aggressive eventually creates space too, because the target of your aggression is likely going to back off.
It may not be super obvious, but the lingering impulses to escape or to aggress can show up in other ways, like in our emotions and our thoughts.

Escape can show up as nervousness, anxiety, thinking about the past, or worrying about the future, like an interaction you had with a coworker or one that's coming up tomorrow. Sorry if I just reminded you of something that's coming up.

Aggression can show up as anger, irritability, frustration at not reaching a goal, snapping at your loved ones (apologize if you need to, by the way), working out in the gym with no relief, or not being able to sleep because you're too activated.
If any of this describes you, you likely have enough mobilization, with sympathetic flight or fight activation in it.

Maybe you don't feel like connecting, and you don't have the energy to mobilize. Instead, you may feel like collapsing. Just falling face first onto your bed and staying there, doing nothing but breathing. You may feel like you need to be alone and turn down the stimulation around you. The lights are too much, sounds are too loud, people are overwhelming, and you can't handle another responsibility.

This is a state of disconnection. If this describes you, you likely have some level of shutdown. At the extreme, it could even look like dissociation. It means your dorsal vagal pathways are overly active, probably because you have some current context, or context from when you were younger, where you could not be safe, could not run away, and could not fight off what was happening.

blocks.h: From primary states to mixed states

blocks.p: Those are the primary states: safety, flight and fight (both sympathetic), and shutdown. You likely have one of these primary states dominant in your system day in and day out.
But these primary states can mix, or combine, to create mixed states, the way primary paint colors mix to create other colors. Red and blue mix to create purple.

blocks.h3: 4. Do you feel ready to have fun with someone else?

blocks.p: What happens when your safety state mixes with sympathetic flight and fight? What happens when you're mobile, but also connected? If you're feeling spontaneous, fun, or imaginative, and you want to share that experience with somebody else, you're likely in the mixed state of play.

Play is mobile, but safe. It's flight and fight mixing with safety, resulting in connection with somebody else, but also competitiveness, spontaneity, and imagination. During play, you're mobile and active with flight and fight, but the safety aspect allows you to stay within the rules of the game, or just general social norms.
Play feels like fun and excitement, but it's a shared experience with somebody else, or multiple people. The connection with a safe other is a really big part of play. It's kind of necessary.

If you're alone, safety can still mix with flight and fight, resulting in motivation, creativity, exercise, and productivity. All of these require energy. Motivation means you're energized to complete a task of some kind. When you're motivated, you can be creative and productive. Motivation feels confident. It feels excited.
Motivation means you take the mobilization of flight and fight and point it in a specific direction, like a painting you're working on or a project you want to get done for your business.

Motivation is not an official polyvagal mixed state. But to me, it seems pretty darn obvious. When you remove the variable of co-regulation from play, you can still be in safety and still be mobilized. Motivation has some elements of play, like the spontaneity and imagination of art, or the challenge of improving on a score, like how many bicep curls you can do this week compared to last week. But motivation lacks the co-regulation with another that play has. All we're doing is removing that variable. Play and motivation are both safety plus flight and fight.
So what happens when safety mixes with shutdown, a defensive state? Just like play and motivation, we get two results: one that depends on a safe other, and one that just needs you to be alone.

blocks.h3: 6. Do you feel reflective and mindful?

blocks.p: Are you curious about your inner world? Do you feel connected with your environment? Are you aware of your senses and how your body responds to them? If so, you likely have access to the mixed state of stillness.

Stillness is the ability to immobilize and be okay with it. It comes from the connection of ventral vagal safety and the immobility of dorsal vagal shutdown. You likely have some stillness right now, as you sit or lie down and read this.

You're in stillness when you can sit down and reflect on life, when you meditate, when you go to sleep, or even when you stand at your work desk. Stillness can be a deep meditative experience, feeling tiny but at one with the universe and in the present moment. But it can also be just sitting down to use the restroom. Both of these require stillness. And by the way, if you're mobile while using the restroom, I would argue you're doing it wrong, and your life might be a lot easier if you immobilize in stillness. Just a life tip.
Stillness is safety and shutdown when you're alone. But what happens when you introduce a safe other into the mix?

blocks.h3: 7. Do you want to connect with someone else?

blocks.p: Do you feel like you could connect with somebody else right now? Could you hold them, look in their eyes, or listen to their feelings? Do you feel ready to receive that and share it with another? If so, you may have access to the intimacy mixed state.

Intimacy is safety and shutdown with a co-regulating other. It doesn't necessarily refer to physical intimacy, but it can include that, like holding hands while watching a movie or massaging your partner at the end of the day. Intimacy can also refer to emotional connection: sharing personal stories and feelings, and connecting on a deeper level with a safe other.

Intimacy isn't quite the right word, because that safe connection with another while immobile is also necessary for other relationships, like a therapeutic one, or a parent holding their child. I don't like the word intimacy for those, but you get the idea. The co-regulation aspect of intimacy is huge, just like it is in play.

If the person you're with is not projecting safety cues, it's hard, maybe impossible, to exist in the intimacy mixed state with them. Likewise, if you're not neurocepting safety cues even though the other person is projecting them, it's hard to settle into intimacy. So a safe other is important, but so is your ability to detect safety through neuroception and then shift into enough safety for intimacy.
Play, motivation, stillness, and intimacy are all mixed states involving safety. But what if safety is not part of the mixed state equation?

blocks.h3: 8. Do you feel out of control or overwhelmed?

blocks.p: Do you feel panicky or rageful? Are your emotions extraordinarily intense, and do you feel like you're losing it? You might be in freeze.

If safety is inactive, you're left with sympathetic flight and fight, and shutdown immobility. Is it possible for the body to be both immobile and mobile? Yes. That's what freeze is: both defensive states active at the same time. Freeze is like having your foot on the accelerator and the brake at the same time. The engine is revving and ready to move the car forward, but the brake is on too.

Freeze is shutdown plus sympathetic. But sympathetic can be flight or fight, so freeze can be flavored more like flight or more like fight, and you might notice a difference in your system. Flavored more like fight, freeze shows up as a chronic underlying rage that explodes when triggered. Flavored by flight, it can show up as a chronic underlying panic that can also trigger into a full-on frozen panic.

Freeze shows up not just as anger, but as rage. Not just as anxiety, but as panic. Not just as stress, but as overwhelm. Freeze can also show up in milder ways, like when your child jumps out of their room and yells, scaring you as you innocently walk down the hallway.

blocks.h3: 9. Do you placate or appease others?

blocks.p: There are two more polyvagal mixed states, though I personally have some questions about these: appeasement and fawn. Both are seen when someone is in an unending, life-threatening scenario, like a hostage situation or an abusive household.

Appeasing is creating a connection with a life-threatening other. It's convincing the other that you're on the same side. The connection acts like a pseudo co-regulation, and it might get the other person, the captor, to reduce danger enough for the captive's needs to be met, or maybe even for the captive to escape. It's hypothesized that appeasement is a combination of all the polyvagal primary states: safety, flight, fight, and shutdown.

Fawn, or placating (I like that word better), is similar. But instead of offering pseudo connection and co-regulation, the placater positions themselves as a non-threat and submissive. They anticipate the needs of the dominant other and largely try to remain invisible and not cause problems.

To me, these seem like behavioral adaptations to a severe and ongoing shutdown or freeze state. If you put others' well-being before your own, you may have some level of these mixed states or behaviors.

The Polyvagal Theory is mostly simple to understand, but applying it is not so obvious. So I invite you to spend the next week or so just practicing identifying your state. You can do it at any given moment, or reflect on your states at the end of the day, or the next morning as you sip a cup of coffee.
Then build from there. We continually build on our knowledge and our application of the Polyvagal Theory, and the next tip is about setting up passive safety cues.
